title: Routes, HTTP Methods, and Status Codes
summary: Map methods and paths to handlers, use GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE the way clients expect, and answer with the right status code.
intro: Roombook answers one request so far. A real API answers dozens: list the rooms, show one, book it, change the booking, cancel it. Each needs a route, the right HTTP method, and the right status code, and clients rely on all three. A browser retries a GET without asking, a phone app retries a POST on a bad connection, and a client's code checks the status before it reads a word of the body. This lesson builds Roombook's routes for rooms and bookings with Go's ServeMux, then goes through the methods one by one, GET and HEAD, POST, PUT and PATCH, and DELETE, and ends with a map of every status code the API sends and when.

steps.title: Routes and path parameters
steps.body:
Every request that reaches Roombook either finds the one handler meant for it, or gets a clear answer that it took a wrong turn. That's routing, and getting it right is what makes an API predictable: the same path always means the same thing, and a mistake gets the status code that says exactly what was wrong.

## Method plus pattern

A **route** pairs a method with a **path pattern** and points to a handler. A pattern can have a **path parameter**, a named piece that stands for any value: in Go, `/v1/rooms/{roomID}` matches `/v1/rooms/3` and `/v1/rooms/42`, and hands your handler the 3 or the 42 by the name `roomID`. Go writes the name with a capital ID, the way Go writes every initialism. The app's whole list of routes is its **route table**, and the router checks each request against it to pick a handler.

```diagram routes-and-methods-route-table
The request matches one row by its method and its path, and that row's handler runs.
```

## Roombook's route table

All of Roombook's routes live in one place, `NewHandler` in `internal/api/routes.go`:

```go
func NewHandler() http.Handler {
	rooms := memory.NewRoomStore()
	bookings := memory.NewBookingStore()

	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /healthz", handleHealthz)

	mux.HandleFunc("GET /v1/rooms", listRooms(rooms))
	mux.HandleFunc("POST /v1/rooms", createRoom(rooms))
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /v1/rooms/{roomID}", getRoom(rooms))
	mux.HandleFunc("PUT /v1/rooms/{roomID}", replaceRoom(rooms))
	mux.HandleFunc("PATCH /v1/rooms/{roomID}", updateRoom(rooms))
	mux.HandleFunc("DELETE /v1/rooms/{roomID}", deleteRoom(rooms))

	mux.HandleFunc("POST /v1/bookings", createBooking(bookings))
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /v1/bookings/{bookingID}", getBooking(bookings))
	mux.HandleFunc("POST /v1/bookings/{bookingID}/cancel", cancelBooking(bookings))

	return mux
}
```

Each pattern starts with its method, then the full path. Every Roombook route sits under `/v1`, for version 1, as the lesson on what an API is described, and `/healthz` stays outside, since it isn't part of the API's contract. Reading the whole table in one function, top to bottom, is one of the nicest things about Go's router.

`listRooms(rooms)` isn't the handler itself: it's a function that takes the room store and returns the handler, which can use the store whenever a request comes in. The stores keep rooms and bookings in memory for now, and the next part shows them.

## Reading a path parameter

`r.PathValue("roomID")` returns the matching piece of the path, always as a string: for `/v1/rooms/3`, it's `"3"`. Roombook's ids are whole numbers, so `parseID` in `internal/api/json.go` turns the text into one:

```go
func parseID(text string) (int64, bool) {
	id, err := strconv.ParseInt(text, 10, 64)
	if err != nil || id <= 0 || strconv.FormatInt(id, 10) != text {
		return 0, false
	}
	return id, true
}
```

`strconv.ParseInt` reads base 10 into 64 bits, and fails on `abc` or `1.5`. The id must be positive, and writing it back must give the same text, which rejects `03` and `+3`, so each room has exactly one address. An id that fails gets **404 Not Found**, the same as an id that's valid but missing. From the client's side, `/v1/rooms/abc` is simply an address where nothing lives.

Every 404 from a handler has the same small body, `{"status":404,"title":"Room not found"}`, sent by `writeError` in `internal/api/json.go`:

```go
type apiError struct {
	Status int    `json:"status"`
	Title  string `json:"title"`
}

// writeError sends an error as a small JSON object, like
// {"status":404,"title":"Room not found"}.
func writeError(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, title string) {
	writeJSON(w, status, apiError{Status: status, Title: title})
}
```

The JSON tags name the fields in the JSON, and the status goes in the body too, so it survives when the body travels without its headers, like in a log. This is a first draft of Roombook's error format. The middleware lesson's own errors use it too, and the lesson on validation and errors grows it into the full Problem Details format, which the lesson on what an API is introduced.

## 404 and 405, for free

A request can miss in two ways, and Go's router answers both by itself. If no pattern matches the path, it answers **404 Not Found**. If the path matches but not the method, like `POST /v1/rooms/1`, it answers **405 Method Not Allowed**, with an `Allow` header listing the methods that work there, built from your own patterns. Both answers are short plain text, unlike Roombook's own JSON errors, as the examples show. The lesson on validation and errors changes them, so every error Roombook sends is JSON.

## The most specific pattern wins

Many routers try routes in the order you add them, so a fixed path added after `{roomID}` would never be reached. Go's doesn't care about order: when two patterns match, the more specific one wins. If Roombook added `GET /v1/rooms/popular`, it would win for that one path, and `{roomID}` would take all the others. Two patterns that are equally specific, like `{roomID}` and `{id}` on the same path, make `HandleFunc` panic as the server starts, so the mistake can't reach a client.

Two more pattern forms are worth knowing: `{path...}` at the end matches the rest of the path, slashes included, and a pattern ending in `/{$}` matches only that exact path, with nothing after it.

examples.title: A room that exists
examples.prompt: With the server running, read room 1.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:27 GMT
Content-Length: 100

{"id":1,"name":"Turing","building":"main-library","capacity":6,"amenities":["whiteboard","screen"]}
examples.explanation: The request matched `GET /v1/rooms/{roomID}`, so the router called `getRoom`'s handler, where `r.PathValue("roomID")` returned `"1"`. `parseID` turned it into the number 1, and the store had room 1, Turing. The JSON is the room as the lesson on what an API is showed it: its id, its name, its building's slug, how many people fit, and its amenities. Notice that `id` is the number 1 in the body: it came from Roombook's own data, not from the path.

examples.title: An id that isn't a number
examples.prompt: Ask for a room whose id is text.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:27 GMT
Content-Length: 40

{"status":404,"title":"Room not found"}
examples.explanation: The path matched `/v1/rooms/{roomID}` with `roomID` set to `"abc"`, but `parseID` said no, so `findRoom` answered with `writeError`. The body repeats the status and gives a title a person can read, and it's JSON, like every other answer Roombook's handlers send, so a client can read it with the same code. `/v1/rooms/99`, a valid id with no room, and `/v1/rooms/03` get exactly the same answer.

examples.title: A method the path doesn't support
examples.prompt: `-X POST` makes curl send POST instead of GET.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Allow: DELETE, GET, HEAD, PATCH, PUT
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:27 GMT
Content-Length: 19

Method Not Allowed
examples.explanation: The path matched four patterns, but none for POST, so the router answered 405 without calling any handler. It built `Allow` from Roombook's own patterns, in alphabetical order, and added HEAD, since every GET route answers HEAD too. A client's developer can read it to see their mistake: to create a room, you POST to `/v1/rooms`, not to one room's address. `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` tells browsers to trust the `Content-Type` and never guess, which Go's error answers always add.

steps.title: GET and HEAD: reading

examples.title: Every room
examples.prompt: Without `-i`, curl prints only the body.
examples.explanation: All three rooms come back inside `items`, in id order, thanks to `sort.Slice`. Run it several times and the order never changes. `json.Marshal` writes JSON with no spaces or line breaks, the smallest form, which is right for programs and hard for people. To read it comfortably, open the same address in a browser, since Firefox and Chrome both lay JSON out neatly, and the lesson on curl and OpenAPI shows jq, the terminal tool most developers use for this.

examples.title: HEAD for the same room
examples.prompt: `-I` sends HEAD and prints the headers it gets back.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:27 GMT
Content-Length: 100
examples.explanation: The status and headers match the GET for room 1, down to `Content-Length: 100`, but no body came back. The router ran the GET handler, which wrote the whole answer, and the server sent only its head. Roombook wrote no code for this. A client that only needs to know whether room 1 exists, or how big its answer is, saves the download. The next lesson adds a header that makes HEAD even more useful: a fingerprint of the room, to compare with a saved copy.

steps.title: POST: creating and actions
steps.body:
Creating is where a client most needs a clear answer: did it work, what's the new thing's id, and where can it be read later. POST is also the one common method that's never safe to repeat, which makes it the method behind most double bookings and double charges on the web.

## Create: 201 with Location

`POST /v1/rooms` creates a room from the JSON in the request's body:

```go
func createRoom(rooms *memory.RoomStore) http.HandlerFunc {
	return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		var in roomInput
		if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&in); err != nil {
			writeError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, "Body is not valid JSON")
			return
		}
		room := rooms.Insert(domain.Room{Name: in.Name, Building: in.Building, Capacity: in.Capacity, Amenities: in.Amenities})
		w.Header().Set("Location", fmt.Sprintf("/v1/rooms/%d", room.ID))
		writeJSON(w, http.StatusCreated, room)
	}
}
```

`r.Body` is the request's body, and `json.NewDecoder(...).Decode(&in)` reads it into `roomInput`, a struct with the four fields a new room has. If the body isn't JSON, the answer is **400 Bad Request**, with the title `Body is not valid JSON`. The next lesson checks bodies more carefully, for their type and their size.

Decoding into its own struct is what keeps a client in its lane. `roomInput` has no `ID` field, so a client that sends `"id": 1` can't overwrite room 1, and any field Roombook doesn't know is simply skipped. The values aren't checked yet: a capacity of 0 would be stored as it is, and the lesson on validation and errors checks every field.

The answer has three parts, and clients use all of them:

- **201 Created**, `http.StatusCreated`: something new exists.
- A `Location` header with the new room's address, `/v1/rooms/4`, where the client can read it from now on.
- The new room in the body, so the client learns its id, and any value the server filled in, without a second request.

## Headers before the status

`w.Header().Set("Location", ...)` comes before `writeJSON` on purpose. `writeJSON` calls `w.WriteHeader`, which sends the status line and every header at once. After that, the headers are already on their way, and changing `w.Header()` does nothing at all: no error, no warning, and no header. The third example shows a `Location` lost exactly that way. Set every header first.

## POST isn't idempotent

Recall from the web course that sending the same POST twice does the work twice. Two identical `POST /v1/rooms` requests make two rooms. For bookings, it's worse. A student taps Book on a train, the request reaches Roombook, the booking is made, and the answer is lost in a tunnel. The app sees a timeout and sends the request again, and now the student holds two bookings. The reliability lesson fixes this with an `Idempotency-Key` header, so Roombook can tell a retry from a new request.

## Actions: POST /v1/bookings/{bookingID}/cancel

Some changes aren't creating a thing or editing a field. Cancelling a booking has rules: only before it starts, only by its owner or staff in that building. It also has effects: the room frees up, and an email goes out. Roombook models it as an **action**: a POST to a path named with a verb, under the booking it acts on.

```go
func cancelBooking(bookings *memory.BookingStore) http.HandlerFunc {
	return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		b, ok := findBooking(w, r, bookings)
		if !ok {
			return
		}
		if b.Status == "cancelled" {
			writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, b)
			return
		}
		writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, bookings.Cancel(b.ID))
	}
}
```

The store's `Cancel` sets the status to `cancelled` and adds 1 to the booking's `version`, which the lesson on constraints and transactions uses to catch two edits that clash. Why not the other methods? Not DELETE, because the booking isn't gone: it stays, cancelled, so the history shows it. Not `PATCH {"status": "cancelled"}`, because then a client could just as easily send `{"status": "confirmed"}` to bring back a booking whose slot someone else now holds. An action runs the process with its rules, and a PATCH edits fields.

This action is safe to retry, even though POST in general isn't: a booking that's already cancelled comes back as it is, unchanged. Design actions this way whenever you can.

## 202: finished later

Some work takes too long to finish while the client waits, like exporting a whole term of bookings to a spreadsheet. The API answers **202 Accepted** at once, with a `Location` pointing at a resource that reports progress. The client checks that address until the work is done, and it then links to the result. Roombook's booking emails work the same way inside the server, with no 202 to the client: the booking gets its 201 straight away, and the email goes out moments later, through the background jobs of the Redis lesson.

examples.title: Creating a room
examples.prompt: `--json` sends its text as the body of a POST, and sets `Content-Type: application/json` for you.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /v1/rooms/4
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:27 GMT
Content-Length: 93

{"id":4,"name":"Hamilton","building":"science-library","capacity":10,"amenities":["screen"]}
examples.explanation: The store gave the new room the next id, 4, and the handler answered 201 with `Location: /v1/rooms/4` and the room itself. The single quotes around the JSON keep the terminal from reading its double quotes and brackets as part of the command. `Location` holds a path, not a full URL, which HTTP allows: the client combines it with the address it called. Run the command again and you get room 5, an identical second room, which is the non-idempotent POST in action.

examples.title: Cancelling a booking
examples.prompt: Booking 1001 is Ada's Algorithms study group in Turing, on Monday 5 October 2026.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:27 GMT
Content-Length: 214

{"id":1001,"roomId":1,"userId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T15:30:00Z","attendees":3,"note":"Algorithms study group","status":"cancelled","version":2,"createdAt":"2026-10-01T09:00:00Z"}
examples.explanation: The action sent no body, since the path says everything: which booking, and what to do. The answer is 200 with the booking, now `"status":"cancelled"` at `"version":2`. Its times are Go `time.Time` values, which turn into JSON in RFC 3339 format, the standard way to write a date and time, ending in `Z` for UTC. Run the command a second time and the answer is the same, still version 2, since the handler returns a cancelled booking without saving it again.

examples.title: A header set too late
examples.prompt: The same create, with the two lines in `createRoom` swapped, so the `Location` line runs after `writeJSON`. The code still compiles, and `go vet` finds nothing.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:39 GMT
Content-Length: 93

{"id":4,"name":"Hamilton","building":"science-library","capacity":10,"amenities":["screen"]}
examples.explanation: The room was made and the status is 201, but `Location` is missing. By the time `Header().Set` ran, `WriteHeader` had already sent the headers, so the change went nowhere, silently. A client that follows `Location` to read the new room now has nothing to follow. This bug is easy to miss, because everything else looks right, and it's why every Go handler sets its headers first. Swap the lines back when you're done.

steps.title: PUT and PATCH: updating
steps.body:
There are two ways to change something that exists, and they behave very differently. Use the wrong one, or build one wrong, and a client that meant to change one field wipes out three others. Knowing exactly what each one promises is what lets clients update safely.

## PUT replaces the whole thing

A **PUT** sends a complete new version of the resource, and the server stores exactly that, in place of the old one:

```go
func replaceRoom(rooms *memory.RoomStore) http.HandlerFunc {
	return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		room, ok := findRoom(w, r, rooms)
		if !ok {
			return
		}
		var in roomInput
		if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&in); err != nil {
			writeError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, "Body is not valid JSON")
			return
		}
		room = domain.Room{ID: room.ID, Name: in.Name, Building: in.Building, Capacity: in.Capacity, Amenities: in.Amenities}
		writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, rooms.Update(room))
	}
}
```

Every field comes from the body, and only the id comes from the room that's there, so the path decides which room, never the body. A field the client leaves out isn't kept. In Go, it isn't even absent: a field the JSON doesn't mention keeps its **zero value**, the value every Go type starts with, so a missing name is `""`, a missing capacity is `0`, and missing amenities are a `nil` slice, which JSON writes as `null`. The third example shows a PUT with only a name doing exactly that. A real API refuses a PUT that's missing required fields, with 422, and the lesson on validation and errors adds that check.

PUT is **idempotent**: sending the same PUT twice leaves the room exactly as one did. That makes it safe for a client to retry.

## PATCH changes some fields

A **PATCH** sends only the changes. Roombook follows **JSON Merge Patch**, a standard set of rules for what a JSON patch means, written down as RFC 7396:

- A field in the patch replaces the current value.
- A field left out stays as it is.
- A field set to `null` is removed, or cleared.
- Arrays are replaced whole. To add an amenity, you send the full new list.
- Objects inside the resource are merged field by field, by the same rules.

A merge patch announces itself with `Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json`, and Roombook accepts that or plain `application/json`.

To know which fields a patch has, the handler decodes it into a struct of **pointers**:

```go
type roomPatch struct {
	Name      *string  `json:"name"`
	Building  *string  `json:"building"`
	Capacity  *int     `json:"capacity"`
	Amenities []string `json:"amenities"`
}
```

A pointer is `nil` when the field wasn't in the JSON, so `nil` means leave it alone, and anything else is a new value. A slice can be `nil` too, so `Amenities` needs no pointer. The handler copies over each field that was sent:

```go
if patch.Name != nil {
	room.Name = *patch.Name
}
if patch.Capacity != nil {
	room.Capacity = *patch.Capacity
}
```

and the same for the building and the amenities, then saves the room with `rooms.Update(room)`.

## Missing or null

JSON can say two different things about a field: it's not there, or it's there and `null`. In a merge patch they mean different things: `{}` changes nothing, and `{"note": null}` clears a booking's note. A pointer can't tell them apart, since `encoding/json` leaves a pointer `nil` in both cases. That's fine for a room, since none of its fields may ever be null, and the lesson on validation and errors turns `{"capacity": null}` into a clear error. For a field that can be cleared, like a booking's note, the handler needs a type that records whether the field was there at all, and the next lesson writes one.

## Is PATCH idempotent?

A merge patch is: sending `{"capacity": 8}` twice still leaves 8. But HTTP doesn't promise it for PATCH in general, since a patch format could say "add 2 to the capacity", which changes the result every time. So the method table in the next part says PATCH isn't idempotent, and clients don't retry one blindly.

## 200 or 204

After an update, an API answers either **200** with the updated resource, or **204 No Content** with no body. Roombook answers 200, so the client sees exactly what's stored, including anything the server changed, like a booking's version number. Pick one and use it for every update.

examples.title: Replacing room 4
examples.prompt: Room 4 is the Hamilton room the POST created. This PUT sends all four fields, with a new capacity and a new amenity.
examples.explanation: `-X PUT` changes the method `--json` would use, which is POST, and keeps the JSON body and its `Content-Type`. The room now holds exactly what the body said: capacity 12, and both amenities. The id is still 4, because it came from the path, not the body. If the server restarted since the POST, room 4 is gone, since the rooms live in memory, and the answer is 404: run the POST from the previous part again first.

examples.title: Patching one field
examples.prompt: `-H` sets a header, here the merge patch's own `Content-Type`, and `-d` sends the body.
examples.explanation: Only the capacity changed, to 8. In `roomPatch`, `Capacity` pointed at 8, and the other three fields were `nil`, so the handler left the name, the building, and the amenities as the PUT set them. `-d` on its own would have sent `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, the type an HTML form uses. This handler doesn't look at the type yet, and the next lesson adds the check that refuses anything but JSON.

examples.title: A PUT that leaves fields out
examples.prompt: The same room, replaced with a body that has only a name.
examples.explanation: The room lost its building, its capacity, and its amenities, and each took its zero value: an empty string, 0, and `null`. The handler did what PUT promises and stored exactly what it got. This is the classic PUT mistake: a client meant to rename the room and sent only the name. The fix is on both sides. Clients use PATCH to change some fields, and the API rejects a PUT that's missing required fields, which the lesson on validation and errors adds with a 422 that names each missing one.

steps.title: DELETE and what each method promises
steps.body:
Deleting is the change you can't take back, and it's also one that clients retry a lot, since a delete that timed out leaves them unsure whether it happened. So it needs an answer that's clear the first time and safe the second.

## 204 No Content

`DELETE /v1/rooms/{roomID}` removes the room and answers **204 No Content**: it worked, and there's nothing to send back.

```go
func deleteRoom(rooms *memory.RoomStore) http.HandlerFunc {
	return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		room, ok := findRoom(w, r, rooms)
		if !ok {
			return
		}
		rooms.Remove(room.ID)
		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
	}
}
```

A 204 can't have a body, so the handler calls `WriteHeader` and writes nothing.

## Soft delete

In memory, Roombook simply removes the room. With a database, it won't. Bookings point at their room, and a booking from last month must still be able to say it was in Turing, so erasing the room would break its history. Instead, Roombook does a **soft delete**: it keeps the room and marks it inactive, and every read skips inactive rooms. To clients, it's gone. To the records, it's still there. The PostgreSQL lesson adds the `active` column that does this.

Deleting has a rule too: a room with upcoming bookings can't be deleted, because the students who booked it would show up to a room that no longer exists in the system. That gets **409 Conflict**, the code for a request that clashes with the current state of the data.

## The second DELETE

After the first DELETE, the room is gone. What should a second, identical DELETE answer? There are two sound choices:

- **204 again**: the client wanted the room gone, and it is.
- **404**: there's no room there to delete.

Either keeps DELETE idempotent, because idempotent means the server ends up in the same state, not that the answer is the same. Roombook answers 404, since nothing is there, and its clients treat a 404 from a DELETE as done. What matters is choosing one and answering it every time, so client developers can rely on it.

## What each method promises

Here's every method Roombook uses, and the promises clients build on:

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Request body | Cacheable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GET | yes | yes | no | yes |
| HEAD | yes | yes | no | yes |
| POST | no | no | yes | rarely |
| PUT | no | yes | yes | no |
| PATCH | no | no | yes | no |
| DELETE | no | yes | no | no |
| OPTIONS | yes | yes | no | no |

- **Safe** methods change nothing, so anything may send them at any time.
- **Idempotent** methods can be retried after a timeout without doing the work twice. A client library may retry GET, PUT, and DELETE by itself, but never POST.
- **Request body** says whether the method carries one. A GET or DELETE with a body is allowed by the rules but has no agreed meaning, and many proxies and libraries drop it, so never design an API that needs one.
- **Cacheable** responses may be stored and reused by browsers and caches, which is how a second visit gets faster. A POST answer can only be reused in rare cases most caches ignore.

## OPTIONS

**OPTIONS** asks a server which methods a path supports. Roombook has no OPTIONS routes, so Go's router treats it like any other method a path doesn't have: 405, with the `Allow` list, as the third example shows. The list is still the answer the client wanted. Browsers send OPTIONS on their own before some requests from other origins, the CORS preflight from the web course, and the security lesson adds the middleware that answers those properly.

examples.title: Deleting room 4
examples.prompt: Room 4 must exist, so run the POST that creates it first if the server restarted.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:27 GMT
examples.explanation: The answer is only a status line and a `Date`: no `Content-Type`, no `Content-Length`, and no body, since a 204 has none. Everything a client needs is in the status: the room is deleted. `GET /v1/rooms` no longer lists it, and its id isn't reused, since the store's counter only goes up. Reusing ids would let an old link to room 4 point at a different room.

examples.title: Deleting it again
examples.prompt: The same command, run a second time.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:27 GMT
Content-Length: 40

{"status":404,"title":"Room not found"}
examples.explanation: `findRoom` found no room 4, so the handler answered 404 before reaching the delete. The server's state is the same as after the first DELETE, which is what makes the method idempotent, even though the status differs. A client that sent the first DELETE, lost the answer, and retried, sees this 404 and knows its goal is met: the room is gone either way.

examples.title: Asking which methods work
examples.prompt: `-X OPTIONS` sends an OPTIONS request for room 1.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Allow: DELETE, GET, HEAD, PATCH, PUT

steps.title: Status codes: the full map
steps.body:
The status code is the first thing a client's code reads, before a single byte of the body. It decides what happens next: show the data, show an error, retry, send the user to log in, or give up. An API that picks its codes carefully lets every client handle every answer correctly without parsing error messages.

## The questions, in order

When a request comes in, an API answers a series of questions, and the first one that fails picks the code. Each later lesson builds one of these checks, but the order already tells you which code to send:

```diagram routes-and-methods-status-codes
Each no leads to its code, and the first one that applies wins.
```

## Every code Roombook sends

| Code | Roombook sends it when |
|---|---|
| 200 OK | a read, an update, or an action worked |
| 201 Created | a POST made a room or a booking |
| 202 Accepted | work was queued, to finish later |
| 204 No Content | a DELETE worked |
| 304 Not Modified | the client's saved copy is still current |
| 400 Bad Request | the request can't be read, like broken JSON |
| 401 Unauthorized | there's no valid login, token, or key |
| 403 Forbidden | the caller is known, but not allowed |
| 404 Not Found | no route matches, or no such room or booking |
| 405 Method Not Allowed | the path exists, but not with that method |
| 409 Conflict | the room is already booked at that time |
| 412 Precondition Failed | an `If-Match` header names an old version |
| 413 Content Too Large | the body is over the size limit |
| 415 Unsupported Media Type | the body isn't JSON |
| 422 Unprocessable Content | the JSON is fine, but a value breaks a rule |
| 429 Too Many Requests | the caller is over its rate limit |
| 500 Internal Server Error | a bug, or a crash |
| 502 Bad Gateway | a service Roombook called gave a broken answer |
| 503 Service Unavailable | Roombook is overloaded, or shutting down |
| 504 Gateway Timeout | a service Roombook called didn't answer in time |

net/http has a constant for each, like `http.StatusConflict` for 409, and handlers use the constants rather than bare numbers. A few have older names, like `http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge` for 413 and `http.StatusUnprocessableEntity` for 422, and the status lines Go writes use those older names too. Only the number counts, and the table uses today's names.

## Pairs that people mix up

- **401 or 403.** 401 means we don't know who you are: log in, or send a valid token. 403 means we know exactly who you are, and you still can't do this, like a member creating a room, which only staff may do.
- **400 or 422.** 400 means the request can't be read at all, like JSON with a missing bracket. 422 means it was read fine, and a value breaks a rule, like booking a room for 6 with 40 attendees.
- **409 or 412.** 409 means the request clashes with the data as it is, like booking a slot that's taken. 412 means the client made its request conditional on a version, with `If-Match`, and the data has changed since it looked, so the server refused to apply a change based on an old copy.

## 4xx or 5xx: who must act

A **4xx** means the client must change something. Sending the same request again gets the same answer, so a client shouldn't retry it as it is. Two are exceptions worth knowing: after a 429, a client waits as long as the `Retry-After` header says and tries again, and after a 409, it can read the latest data and then decide.

A **5xx** means the server failed, and the request itself may have been fine. A retry a little later may work, especially after a 502, 503, or 504. But only retry what's safe to repeat: a GET, a PUT, a DELETE, or a POST with an idempotency key, from the reliability lesson. Retrying a plain POST after a 504 can book a room twice, since the first request may have worked before the answer was lost.

## Never 200 for an error

Some APIs answer every request with 200, and put `{"error": "..."}` in the body. Don't. Caches store a 200 and hand the error to the next person, monitoring counts it as a success, and every client has to read the body to find out that something went wrong. In Go, the status is the argument to `WriteHeader`, which `writeJSON` and `writeError` take as their own `status` argument, and a handler that writes a body without calling `WriteHeader` first sends 200. Roombook's errors also repeat their status in the body, and the lesson on validation and errors grows them into the full Problem Details format.

The next lesson reads every part of a request: the path, the query string, the headers, and the body.

recap:
- A route is a method plus a path pattern, like GET /v1/rooms/{roomID}, and Go's router picks the most specific match, whatever the order.
- r.PathValue returns path parameters as strings, and an id that isn't valid gets a 404, like one that doesn't exist.
- The router answers 404 and 405 with Allow by itself, in plain text, and answers HEAD with the GET handler.
- GET and HEAD only read, so crawlers, caches, and retries can send them at any time.
- POST creates with 201 and a Location header, set before WriteHeader, runs actions like cancel, and isn't safe to repeat.
- PUT replaces the whole resource, so missing fields become zero values, and PATCH with pointer fields changes only what's sent.
- DELETE answers 204, Roombook soft-deletes rooms, and a second DELETE gets 404 every time.
- 4xx means the client must change the request, 5xx means the server failed, and an error never gets 200.
